0.title: All Is Vanity — and Yet
0.overview:
Ecclesiastes is the most daring book in Scripture. The Preacher — Qohelet in Hebrew, the Assembler, the one who gathers wisdom and weighs experience — opens not with a doxology but with a diagnosis: hebel. The word is usually translated “vanity,” but it means literally “breath” or “vapor.” Mist. It appears thirty-eight times in twelve chapters. The Preacher is not being melodramatic. He is being precise.

What is hebel? It is the quality of things that look solid but dissolve when grasped. Not evil — vaporous. Not sinful — ephemeral. The river runs to the sea and the sea is never full. The sun rises and the sun sets. Generations come and go and the earth endures indifferent. You pour your life into work and a stranger inherits it. You accumulate wisdom and die alongside the fool. This is not despair; it is diagnosis. Under the sun, without God, this is what is simply and factually true.

Timothy Keller often observed that Ecclesiastes is the most postmodern book in the Bible because it takes the secular experience with total seriousness. The Preacher does not argue against life without God from the outside — he grants the premise and follows it ruthlessly to its conclusion. Pleasure (chapter 2). Wealth and great projects (chapter 2). Wisdom itself (chapter 1). Justice perverted (chapter 3). Loneliness (chapter 4). Religious performance without heart (chapter 5). Each time, the verdict is the same: vanity, and a striving after wind.

But Ecclesiastes is not the counsel of despair. It is a diagnostic instrument wielded by a faithful God to prepare his people for good news. The path from vanity to meaning runs straight through the cross and out the other side. Jesus Christ, the eternal Son, entered fully into hebel. He was born of a woman, born under the law, born into the cycles of toil and grief and death the Preacher catalogues. He asked the Preacher’s ultimate question from the cross: My God, my God, why? And God answered from the empty tomb. The resurrection is God’s answer to every chapter of Ecclesiastes. There is work that is not in vain in the Lord (1 Cor. 15:58). There is an inheritance that does not perish (1 Pet. 1:4). There is a joy no one can take away (John 16:22). There is a wisdom that is not a striving after wind — it is Christ himself, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3).

Read Ecclesiastes slowly. Let it expose every substitute saviour you have been carrying. Let the weight of hebel press on you until you feel how hollow life is without God. And then hear the gospel again — not as a comfortable habit, but as the only answer to a question Qohelet spent twelve chapters asking.

1.title: Vanity of Vanities
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem. <sup>2</sup>Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity. <sup>3</sup>What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? <sup>4</sup>A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. <sup>5</sup>The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to its place where it rises. <sup>6</sup>The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. <sup>7</sup>All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again. <sup>8</sup>All things are full of weariness; a man cannot utter it; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing. <sup>9</sup>What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun. <sup>10</sup>Is there a thing of which it is said, “See, this is new”? It has been already in the ages before us. <sup>11</sup>There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be any remembrance of things that are to come among those who come after. <sup>12</sup>I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem. <sup>13</sup>And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with. <sup>14</sup>I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind. <sup>15</sup>What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted. <sup>16</sup>I said in my heart, “I have acquired great wisdom, surpassing all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge.” <sup>17</sup>And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also is but a striving after wind. <sup>18</sup>For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.
1.overview:
The Preacher drops his thesis like a stone into still water: hebel. Thirty-eight times this word will surface in the chapters that follow. It means breath, vapor, mist — not meaninglessness in some abstract philosophical sense, but the particular anguish of grasping something that looks solid and finding it dissolve in your hand. Qohelet is not a cynic; he is a mourner. He has looked hard at the world and loves it enough to grieve what it cannot deliver.

The images he chooses are hauntingly beautiful: the sun that races and returns, the wind that spirals on its circuits, the rivers that pour forever into an ocean that never fills. Creation is not broken — it is relentless. And relentlessness without arrival is its own kind of anguish. The eye is never satisfied with seeing. The ear is never filled with hearing. This is not a description of evil; it is a description of finitude — of creatures who were made for eternity living inside time.

Wisdom, the Preacher discovers, does not resolve the problem. It deepens it. The more clearly you see, the more you grieve. This is not an argument against wisdom; it is an argument against treating wisdom as a saviour. And it is here that Ecclesiastes begins its long, patient work of clearing the ground — pulling up every false root, exposing every insufficient anchor, until only one foundation remains: the God who stands outside the circuits, who was before the first generation and will be after the last, who gives meaning not as an idea but as a Person. Jesus Christ is the Wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24) — and unlike Qohelet’s wisdom, he does not increase sorrow. He bears it, and transforms it into glory.

verseByVerse.quote: “Vanity of vanities … All is vanity.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The superlative form — vanity of vanities — is Hebrew idiom for the most absolute vanity possible, just as “Song of Songs” means the greatest of all songs. From the first breath, Qohelet refuses false comfort. He will not begin with what we wish were true; he begins with what he has actually observed. This is a mark of courage and pastoral love. A doctor who lies about a diagnosis does not love his patient. The Preacher loves us enough to tell the truth.

The word hebel is also the name Abel — the first man to die, whose life was the shortest in Genesis. Whether this is intentional wordplay or not, the echo is striking: the vapour of human life is as old as the first grave. And yet the God who stood at Abel’s grave is the same God who will raise the dead. Hebel is not the last word in Scripture — resurrection is.

verseByVerse.quote: “What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word gain (Hebrew yitron) is a commercial term: profit, surplus, what remains after all the accounts are settled. Qohelet is asking a bookkeeper’s question: when you total up a life of labour, what is left over? And the cosmos itself answers: nothing accumulates. The sun races and returns to its starting point. The wind makes its circuit and arrives where it began. The rivers pour themselves out and the sea absorbs it all and shows nothing for it. The universe runs and runs and goes nowhere.

This is not fatalism but revelation. The creation is telling us something about our nature: we were not made to find our yitron in toil under the sun. We were made for something the sun cannot give. The very restlessness of creation echoes Augustine: our heart is restless until it rests in Thee.

verseByVerse.quote: “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Desire is the Preacher’s great subject. Not desire as sin — desire as structure. We are built to want. The eye opens in the morning hungry for something it cannot name; it closes at night having seen much and been filled by nothing. This is not a malfunction. It is the signature of a soul made for God pressing itself against the world and finding the world too small.

C.S. Lewis called this the argument from desire: the fact that we hunger proves there is food; the fact that we long for eternity proves there is an eternal country. Qohelet feels the hunger acutely but has not yet seen the feast. He is writing from the far side of the cross, waiting for what he cannot quite name. We read him from the near side, knowing the name: Jesus, the bread of life, who said whoever comes to me shall not hunger (John 6:35).

verseByVerse.quote: “All is vanity and a striving after wind.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher turns his formidable royal resources toward wisdom: position, wealth, access, leisure, the best minds of his age. He searches out everything done under heaven. The verdict is devastating: it is an “unhappy business” — literally a bad task, a miserable occupation. Not because knowledge is bad but because knowledge gained under the sun, without the Author of all things at the centre, only reveals the depth of what is crooked and the breadth of what is lacking.

“What is crooked cannot be made straight” (v. 15). This is not pessimism — it is soteriology. The Preacher has discovered the doctrine of total depravity from the inside. No human wisdom can straighten what sin has bent. That required a craftsman from outside the system — the Word who was with God, who became flesh, who will one day make all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: “In much wisdom is much vexation.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the Preacher’s first great paradox: wisdom, which should bring peace, brings grief. The more clearly you see, the more you mourn. This is not an argument against wisdom — Qohelet values wisdom throughout the book. It is an argument against the idolatry of wisdom, the notion that understanding is a substitute for redemption. The wise man sees his own limits more clearly than the fool does. He sees the crooked places. He sees the graves. He sees that more knowledge only extends the horizon of mystery.

This is why Paul calls the cross “foolishness to the Greeks” (1 Cor. 1:23). The Greeks wanted wisdom; the cross appeared to be its opposite. But God’s foolishness is wiser than human wisdom. Only in Christ — the Wisdom of God incarnate — does wisdom stop increasing sorrow and begin producing joy. He is the end of the Preacher’s search.

1.theology:
Hebel and the Doctrine of Creation’s Groaning. Reformed theology insists that creation, though good in origin, is now subjected to futility — not by its own will but by God’s sovereign decree in response to the fall (Rom. 8:20). Qohelet is not contradicting Genesis when he says all is vanity; he is describing the world east of Eden with agonising accuracy. The circuits of the sun, the rivers that never fill the sea — these are the groans of a creation waiting for liberation.

But Paul continues the sentence: “in hope” (Rom. 8:20). The subjection is not final. The groaning is not permanent. Creation was subjected in hope because the same God who subjected it has promised its liberation through the sons of God — those reborn in Christ, heirs of the new creation. Ecclesiastes chapter 1 is Romans 8:20 in poetry form. The Preacher feels the groaning; Paul names the hope. Together they point to the day when hebel ends and glory begins.
1.examples:
Then: Qohelet observed kings, scholars, and merchants of ancient Israel and the surrounding nations pouring their lives into accumulation — gold, armies, libraries, monuments. Egypt’s pharaohs built tombs for their immortality. Solomon himself built a temple and a palace and wrote a thousand songs. And yet: no remembrance of former things (v. 11). The monuments crumble; the names are forgotten. The Preacher watched it happen from the most privileged seat in the ancient world and refused to pretend otherwise.

Now: We live in the most productive civilisation in human history, and the Preacher’s question presses harder than ever: What does man gain? Your social media following vanishes when the platform dies. Your career achievements will not survive three generations of memory. The urgent emails of today are forgotten by next year. This is not morbid — it is liberating. Because once you stop trying to build your significance in the circuits of the sun, you are free to receive it as a gift from the God who holds the sun in place. In Christ, your labour is not in vain (1 Cor. 15:58) — not because you made it significant, but because he did.

2.title: The Great Experiment
2.text: <sup>1</sup>I said in my heart, “Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself.” But behold, this also was vanity. <sup>2</sup>I said of laughter, “It is mad,” and of pleasure, “What use is it?” <sup>3</sup>I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine — my heart still guiding me with wisdom — and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life. <sup>4</sup>I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself. <sup>5</sup>I made myself gardens and parks, and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees. <sup>6</sup>I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees. <sup>7</sup>I bought male and female slaves, and had slaves who were born in my house. I had also great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem. <sup>8</sup>I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, both men and women, and many concubines, the delight of the sons of man. <sup>9</sup>So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me. <sup>10</sup>And whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my reward for all my toil. <sup>11</sup>Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun. <sup>12</sup>So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly. <sup>13</sup>Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness. <sup>14</sup>The wise man has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them. <sup>15</sup>Then I said in my heart, “What happens to the fool will happen to me also. Why then have I been so very wise?” And I said in my heart that this also is vanity. <sup>16</sup>For of the wise man, even as of the fool, there is no enduring remembrance, seeing that in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. How the wise man dies just like the fool! <sup>17</sup>So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind. <sup>18</sup>I hated all my toil in which I toil under the sun, seeing that I must leave it to the man who comes after me, <sup>19</sup>and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity. <sup>20</sup>So I turned about and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil of my labors under the sun, <sup>21</sup>because sometimes a person who has toiled with wisdom and knowledge and skill must leave everything to be enjoyed by someone who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil. <sup>22</sup>What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun? <sup>23</sup>For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity. <sup>24</sup>There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God, <sup>25</sup>for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment? <sup>26</sup>For to the one who pleases him God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to one who pleases God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the Preacher’s great experiment. He is not a pessimist by temperament — he is a scientist of human experience. And so he tests everything with ruthless honesty. Pleasure: he withholds nothing from his eyes. Projects: he builds on a scale no private citizen could dream of. Wisdom: he refuses to abandon it even while testing folly. The result is the most comprehensive laboratory failure in the history of human aspiration. “Behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind.”

What makes chapter 2 so devastating is the verse that follows the verdict: wisdom remains with me (v. 9). Qohelet did not lose his mind in the experiment. He saw clearly the whole time. Wisdom watched as pleasure failed to satisfy. Wisdom noted as the great projects were completed and the emptiness remained. Wisdom observed that the wise man and the fool share the same grave. And wisdom could not fix any of it.

And then — glory. At the bottom of the chapter, where despair has reached its lowest point, the Preacher makes the most startling turn in the book: There is nothing better for a person than to eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God (v. 24). Ordinary pleasure — bread and cup and honest work — received as gift from God’s hand, is the beginning of wisdom’s true fruit. This is not resignation; it is eucharist. Every simple joy, received with gratitude, is a taste of the One who is himself Joy. The empty hands that could hold nothing “under the sun” are filled the moment they are opened toward God.

verseByVerse.quote: “I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher does not stumble into pleasure — he chooses it deliberately as a controlled experiment. He is the wealthiest, most powerful man of his age, and he turns all of that toward the question: Can pleasure satisfy? The answer takes the rest of the chapter. The verdict comes quickly: “this also was vanity.” Laughter is “mad” — not evil, but unhinged from reality. Pleasure detached from God is noise that echoes in an empty room.

Jesus said, “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10). The Preacher’s experiment is searching for abundance in the wrong direction — downward into sensation rather than upward toward the Giver. Every pleasure that fails to satisfy is a signpost pointing somewhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: “I became great and surpassed all who were before me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scope of Qohelet’s achievement is staggering: houses, vineyards, gardens, parks, pools, servants, herds, silver and gold, singers, concubines. He is describing Solomon at the apex of his power — a civilisation-builder. And wisdom remained with him through it all (v. 9). He saw exactly what he was doing. He kept his accounts clearly. He knew the price of everything and gained it. And then: “all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun” (v. 11).

The phrase “nothing to be gained” returns to chapter 1’s opening question. After the greatest achievement experiment in history, the answer is: no profit. This is not because the things were evil; it is because they were finite, and a finite thing cannot fill an infinite hunger. Augustine’s restless heart cannot be stilled by anything that was made. Only the Maker can do that.

verseByVerse.quote: “The same event happens to all of them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is genuinely better than folly — Qohelet never denies this. The wise man has his eyes open; the fool walks in darkness. But the advantage is temporary. Death levels all accounts. The wise man and the fool share the same grave, and in generations to come, neither will be remembered. This is not cynicism; it is the honest observation of a man who has watched history long enough to see how quickly reputations dissolve.

The answer to this is not to stop valuing wisdom but to stop trusting wisdom to save you. Wisdom cannot prevent the one event that ends all events. Only resurrection can do that — and resurrection is not a product of wisdom but a gift of grace. The one who rose from the dead was not the wisest man but the obedient Son, who received from his Father the life that death cannot touch.

verseByVerse.quote: “So I hated life.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the abyss. The Preacher does not soften it. He hated life. He hated his toil. He despaired. Why? Because he saw with perfect clarity that he would die and leave everything to a stranger who might be a fool. All the accumulated wisdom and wealth would pass to hands he could not choose or control. The labour of decades gone in a moment of inheritance.

This is not a passage to rush past. Qohelet is voicing what many people feel and few say aloud. The Psalms of lament do the same — they do not pretend the darkness is not dark. And the God who inspired these words is the God who enters darkness. “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” is the cry of a man who felt exactly what Qohelet describes. Jesus descended into our hebel so that we would not descend into it alone.

verseByVerse.quote: “This also, I saw, is from the hand of God.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The turn is sudden and luminous. After the darkness, a small but brilliant light: ordinary joy — eating, drinking, finding satisfaction in honest work — is a gift from the hand of God. Not the achievement. Not the accumulation. The enjoyment. And enjoyment, unlike achievement, cannot be manufactured; it can only be received. This is the first eucharistic moment in the book, and it points forward to every Lord’s Table: simple bread and wine, received from the hand of God, become the most significant meal in human history.

Verse 26 is startling: God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to the one who pleases him. This is not works-righteousness; it is covenant faithfulness. The one who pleases God supremely is Jesus Christ, the Beloved Son, and in him we become those who please God (Eph. 1:6). All the wisdom, knowledge, and joy Qohelet sought are ours as gifts — in the one who is himself the wisdom and joy of God.

2.theology:
The Insufficiency of Created Goods. Reformed theology has always maintained a careful distinction between created goods — which are genuinely good, given by God for human flourishing — and the idolatrous use of those goods as replacements for God. Calvin called the human heart a “perpetual factory of idols.” Ecclesiastes 2 is that factory running at full capacity. Every good thing Qohelet tests — pleasure, beauty, achievement, wisdom — is a genuine good. The failure is not in the things but in what is demanded of them: ultimate satisfaction, meaning, permanence. They cannot deliver what only God can give.

The corrective is not asceticism but eucharist: receiving good things as gifts from the hand of God (v. 24). The Reformers rediscovered this. Luther’s theology of the cross insists that God is found not in the heights of mystical ascent but in the ordinary: bread, wine, water, Word. The Preacher reaches the same conclusion: ordinary joy, received from God’s hand with thanksgiving, is the beginning of the good life — not its inferior substitute.
2.examples:
Then: Solomon’s experiment in chapter 2 maps almost perfectly onto the biographies of the ancient world’s great achievers. Alexander the Great wept because there were no more worlds to conquer — and died at thirty-two, leaving his empire to be torn apart by men who did not earn it, exactly as Qohelet feared (v. 19). The Romans built aqueducts and coliseums and stadiums that still stand — but their builders are forgotten. The experiment has been run at every scale of human achievement, and the verdict is always the same: vanity.

Now: The TED Talk version of the good life is Ecclesiastes 2 retold as optimism: find your passion, achieve your goals, build your legacy. But the Preacher has already run that experiment with far greater resources than any of us possess. The answer is not to stop building or to stop enjoying — it is to stop demanding that your building justify your existence. When you receive your work as a gift from God and your enjoyment as a grace, something shifts. The work is the same; the posture is everything. That shift is what the gospel produces: you no longer have to make yourself significant because you already are — in Christ, who chose you before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4).

3.title: A Time for Everything
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven: <sup>2</sup>a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted; <sup>3</sup>a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; <sup>4</sup>a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; <sup>5</sup>a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing; <sup>6</sup>a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; <sup>7</sup>a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; <sup>8</sup>a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace. <sup>9</sup>What gain has the worker from his toil? <sup>10</sup>I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with. <sup>11</sup>He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end. <sup>12</sup>I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live; <sup>13</sup>also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in his toil — this is God's gift to man. <sup>14</sup>I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him. <sup>15</sup>That which is, already has been; that which is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away. <sup>16</sup>Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness. <sup>17</sup>I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work. <sup>18</sup>I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts. <sup>19</sup>For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity. <sup>20</sup>All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return. <sup>21</sup>Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes downward to the earth? <sup>22</sup>So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?
3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens with one of the most beautiful passages in the Bible — and one of the most misread. The poem of times and seasons is not an invitation to passive fatalism (“everything happens for a reason, so relax”). It is a declaration of sovereign order: every moment, every transition, every ending and beginning is held in the hands of a God who makes everything beautiful in its time. The Preacher is not counselling indifference; he is pointing to Providence.

Verse 11 is the hinge of the entire book: He has put eternity into man’s heart. This is the diagnosis that explains every chapter. We are creatures with an eternal appetite living in a temporal world. No arrangement of temporal things — no perfect season, no ideal moment, no greatest achievement — can satisfy a heart built for what lies beyond the sun. The ache is not a defect; it is a design feature. God placed eternity in us so that we would seek him — the Eternal One who enters time in Jesus Christ.

And then the gospel resolution: whatever God does endures forever (v. 14). Our work is vanity; God’s work is permanent. This is not discouragement but liberation. You do not have to make your work permanent — you cannot. But you can participate in God’s work, which is. And in Christ, your work done in him and for him is taken up into his eternal purposes. The wood, hay, and stubble will burn; the gold refined in the fire will endure (1 Cor. 3:12–15).

verseByVerse.quote: “For everything there is a season.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poem moves in pairs of opposites: birth and death, planting and uprooting, weeping and laughing, war and peace. Fourteen pairs in all. The structure itself makes the point: life is not monotone but rhythmic, not chaotic but ordered. There is a grain to reality that wisdom learns to read. The fool fights the season; the wise person discerns it.

Jesus read the times perfectly. He wept at Lazarus’s tomb (a time to mourn) and turned water to wine at a wedding (a time to rejoice). He was silent before Pilate (a time for silence) and spoke with the authority of God in the temple (a time to speak). His life was the perfect navigation of seasons — and the cross was the moment when, in the fullness of time, God sent his Son (Gal. 4:4), the ultimate kairos breaking into chronos.

verseByVerse.quote: “He has put eternity into man’s heart.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is perhaps the single most important verse in Ecclesiastes. It explains everything: why pleasure cannot satisfy, why achievement fades, why wisdom increases sorrow. God has wired us for infinity. The word eternity here (Hebrew olam) means the eternal order, the sense that there is something beyond the horizon of time. God placed this sense in us deliberately — not as cruelty but as compass.

Augustine’s our heart is restless until it rests in Thee is the New Testament commentary on this verse. The restlessness is the gift. Every unsatisfied longing is God’s fingerprint on the soul, pointing beyond the sun. And Jesus, who is “the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13:8), is the only object large enough to fill what God placed in the human heart.

verseByVerse.quote: “Whatever God does endures forever.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher’s conclusion from the poem of times is not resignation but a radical reorientation: stop trying to make your work endure, and start participating in God’s work, which already does. “God seeks what has been driven away” (v. 15) — a phrase that points forward to the seeking God of the parables, the Father who runs toward the prodigal, the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine. God’s work is redemption, and redemption endures forever.

This is the foundation of Reformed theology’s doctrine of the perseverance of the saints. God’s work in his people endures forever because God’s work endures forever. What he begins, he completes (Phil. 1:6). The seasons change, but the Sovereign does not.

verseByVerse.quote: “God will judge the righteous and the wicked.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher turns from beauty to injustice without flinching. In the very places where justice should reign — the courts, the council chambers — wickedness sits enthroned. This is not a new observation; it is the oldest wound in human society. And Qohelet’s answer is neither revolution nor cynicism but eschatology: God will judge.

This verse is a seed of the doctrine of final judgment that flowers fully in the New Testament. Every injustice that goes uncorrected, every oppressor who dies in comfort, every innocent person who suffers without redress — all of it is seen and recorded by a God for whom there is a time for every work. The cross is where God’s justice fell on his own Son so that his mercy could reach us. The final judgment is where the full account is settled. The Preacher is right: the time is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: “All are from the dust, and to dust all return.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher presses the mortality argument to its limit: without the certainty of resurrection, what distinguishes man from beast? Both breathe, both die, both return to dust. His question in verse 21 — who knows whether the human spirit ascends? — is honest and searching, not cynical. He is testing the limits of what can be known “under the sun.” And from under the sun, unaided, the answer is: we cannot be sure.

But we read this east of Easter. The resurrection of Jesus Christ is God’s definitive answer to verse 21: the spirit of the Son of Man ascended. And because he is the firstfruits, all who are in him will follow (1 Cor. 15:20–23). The question Qohelet could not answer, God answered on Easter morning.

3.theology:
The Sovereignty of God over Time. Reformed theology has always insisted that God’s sovereignty is not a general oversight of history but a particular ordering of every moment. The Westminster Confession declares that God “ordains whatsoever comes to pass.” Ecclesiastes 3 is the wisdom literature version of this doctrine: there is a time for every matter under heaven, and that time is not accidental but appointed.

Crucially, this does not eliminate human responsibility or reduce life to fatalism. The Preacher still calls people to discernment: to know when to speak and when to be silent, when to plant and when to harvest. Wisdom is the art of reading God’s times and moving with them rather than against them. This is the partnership of sovereignty and responsibility that runs through all of Reformed ethics: God ordains the ends and the means, and we are the means. The seasons are appointed; how we navigate them is our calling.
3.examples:
Then: Israel’s history was a classroom in reading God’s times. There was a time to go to war (Deborah, David) and a time to be still (Jehoshaphat before the invading armies). There was a time to build (Solomon’s temple) and a time to let it fall (the Babylonian exile). The prophets were masters of discerning the season — Isaiah announcing comfort when judgment had run its course, Jeremiah calling for surrender when resistance was futile. The nation suffered most when it could not read the times.

Now: We live in a culture that refuses seasons. We medicate grief so we can skip mourning. We scroll through entertainment to avoid silence. We rush to resolution before lamentation has done its work. Ecclesiastes 3 gives us permission — even commands us — to inhabit each season fully. There is a time to weep, and skipping it does not bring joy sooner; it only defers it and diminishes it. Jesus wept at Lazarus’s tomb even knowing he was about to raise him. Let the season be what it is. Trust the God who holds every season in his hands, and receive joy when it comes as the pure gift it is.

4.title: The Burden of Going It Alone
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them! On the side of their oppressors there was power, and there was no one to comfort them. <sup>2</sup>And I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive. <sup>3</sup>But better than both is he who has not yet been and has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun. <sup>4</sup>Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind. <sup>5</sup>The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh. <sup>6</sup>Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind. <sup>7</sup>Again, I saw vanity under the sun: <sup>8</sup>one person who has no other, either son or brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches, so that he never asks, “For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?” This also is vanity and an unhappy business. <sup>9</sup>Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. <sup>10</sup>For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up! <sup>11</sup>Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone? <sup>12</sup>And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him — a threefold cord is not quickly broken. <sup>13</sup>Better was a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knew how to take advice. <sup>14</sup>For he went from prison to the throne, though in his own kingdom he had been born poor. <sup>15</sup>I saw all the living who move about under the sun, along with that youth who was to stand in the king’s place. <sup>16</sup>There was no end of all the people, all of whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 moves through three related meditations on the cost of isolation: the loneliness of the oppressed, the futility of solitary ambition, and the wisdom of companionship. The Preacher is a compassionate observer. He sees the tears of the oppressed and notes with sorrow that there is no one to comfort them. This is not abstract social commentary — it is pastoral attention to the specific weight of being alone in suffering.

The paean to companionship in verses 9–12 is one of the most beloved passages in Ecclesiastes — and rightly so. “Two are better than one.” The reasons are intensely practical: shared labour yields better reward, a fallen companion is lifted, two keep each other warm, two can resist what one cannot. The Preacher is not romantic about friendship; he is honest about its necessity. Isolation is not spiritual strength — it is vulnerability dressed up as independence.

The “threefold cord” of verse 12 has been rightly understood by the Christian tradition as pointing to the third party in every true human relationship: God himself. A marriage, a friendship, a community bound together in Christ is not a cord of two strands but three. And the risen Christ who promised to be present wherever two or three gather in his name (Matt. 18:20) is the strongest strand of all — the one who does not break.

verseByVerse.quote: “They had no one to comfort them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The repetition is deliberate and devastating: “no one to comfort them” twice in one verse. The Preacher sees power arrayed on one side and tears on the other, and the thing that breaks him is not the power but the absence of comfort. Oppression is terrible; comfortless oppression is unbearable. He goes so far as to call the already-dead more fortunate — a hyperbolic expression of grief, not a theological argument for death’s superiority.

The God of Scripture is the God of all comfort (2 Cor. 1:3). He sees the tears Qohelet sees. He heard the cry of his people in Egypt when there was no human comforter. And in Christ, he sent the Paraclete — literally the Comforter, the one called alongside — to be present in every place of comfortless grief. The verse that breaks the Preacher’s heart is answered by Pentecost.

verseByVerse.quote: “All toil and all skill in work come from a man’s envy of his neighbor.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
A startling diagnosis of the engine behind human productivity: envy. Not always conscious, not always ugly — but the comparing gaze, the need to match or surpass, the restlessness produced by watching a neighbour’s success. The Preacher has looked at the marketplace and seen that much of what passes for ambition is actually competition anxiety. And competition anxiety, unlike genuine calling, is a “striving after wind.”

The gospel releases us from this. When your identity is secured in Christ — loved, chosen, adopted before the foundation of the world — you no longer need to define yourself against your neighbour. You can celebrate his success without feeling diminished by it. The freedom from envy is one of the least celebrated but most practical fruits of justification by grace alone.

verseByVerse.quote: “For whom am I toiling?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 8 is one of the loneliest in the Old Testament: a man with no family, no heir, no companion — working without end, eyes never satisfied with wealth, never stopping to ask why. The Preacher calls it “vanity and an unhappy business.” The Hebrew word for unhappy here is painful: it means bad, grievous, evil. Purposeless solitary toil is not admirable self-sufficiency; it is a kind of walking death.

This verse is a pastoral gift to workaholics. The Preacher does not condemn work — he celebrates it. But work without relationship, work that has become its own end rather than a gift offered to God and neighbour, is vanity. The question “for whom am I toiling?” is the question every person needs to ask. The answer that rescues is: for the glory of God and the good of others (1 Cor. 10:31).

verseByVerse.quote: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the darkness of oppression and lonely ambition, this passage shines. The Preacher lists five practical advantages of companionship: better return on labour, mutual help in falling, shared warmth, strength against enemies, and the unbreakable threefold cord. Each example is drawn from the texture of daily life — walking, sleeping, travelling, fighting. Genuine community is not a luxury but a survival mechanism woven into creation.

The church is the community God built for this purpose. It is not a gathering of individuals who happen to share a building on Sunday; it is the body of Christ, members one of another (Rom. 12:5), designed to lift the fallen, warm the cold, and withstand together what none could withstand alone. Every time the church functions as it was designed to, it is the threefold cord in action.

verseByVerse.quote: “Better was a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final vignette of the chapter is about the transience of popular acclaim. A young man rises from poverty and prison to the throne — wisdom over status, merit over birth. The crowds celebrate. And then the next generation comes and does not rejoice in him either. Political popularity is the most volatile of all currencies. The Preacher has watched enough successions to know: the crowd’s acclaim is worth exactly what it costs them to give it — nothing.

This points forward to Palm Sunday. The crowd that shouted “Hosanna” on Sunday shouted “Crucify him” on Friday. Human acclaim is hebel. But the commendation that endures is the Father’s: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). Seek that verdict, and you have found the only approval that will never reverse.

4.theology:
The Image of God and Human Solidarity. Genesis 1:26–27 reveals that God created humanity in his image — and from the beginning, that image was communal: “male and female he created them.” The triune God who is himself a community of love created beings who bear his image most fully in relationship. Ecclesiastes 4 is the wisdom literature version of this truth: isolation is not godly; it is sub-human. The Preacher observes that solitary toil without purpose or companionship is “vanity and an unhappy business” — a failure to live as image-bearers were designed to live.

The doctrine of the church as the body of Christ (1 Cor. 12) is the New Testament elaboration of the Preacher’s threefold cord. We are not designed to be lone-ranger Christians any more than a hand is designed to function detached from a body. Reformed ecclesiology has always insisted that you cannot have God as your Father if you refuse the church as your mother (Calvin). The Preacher’s practical wisdom and Calvin’s theological conviction point to the same reality: God made us for community, and the community he makes possible in Christ is the fullest expression of that design.
4.examples:
Then: Israel’s greatest failures often came from broken community. Saul’s isolation from Samuel after the breach at Gilgal left him without a prophetic voice and spiralled into paranoia. David’s sin with Bathsheba happened on an evening when his companions had gone to war and he remained alone on the rooftop. Elijah’s despair under the broom tree (“I alone am left”) was the cry of a man who had lost his threefold cord. God’s remedy was not a theology lecture but food, rest, and a companion — Elisha.

Now: Loneliness is the epidemic beneath every other epidemic of our age. We are more connected digitally and more isolated relationally than any generation in history. The Preacher’s wisdom is urgent: two are better than one. Find your Elisha. Be someone’s Elisha. Join the body of Christ not as a consumer of spiritual services but as a member who lifts and is lifted, who warms and is warmed. The threefold cord is not a metaphor — it is a survival instruction for the human soul.

5.title: The Fear of God
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil. <sup>2</sup>Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few. <sup>3</sup>For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words. <sup>4</sup>When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow. <sup>5</sup>It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay. <sup>6</sup>Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands? <sup>7</sup>For when dreams increase and words grow many, there is vanity; but God is the one you must fear. <sup>8</sup>If you see in a province the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness, do not be amazed at the matter, for the high official is watched by a higher, and there are yet higher ones over them. <sup>9</sup>But this is gain for a land in every way: a king committed to cultivated fields. <sup>10</sup>He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income; this also is vanity. <sup>11</sup>When goods increase, they increase who eat them, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes? <sup>12</sup>Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep. <sup>13</sup>There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches were kept by their owner to his hurt, <sup>14</sup>and those riches were lost in a bad venture. And he is father of a son, but he has nothing in his hand. <sup>15</sup>As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry away in his hand. <sup>16</sup>This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind? <sup>17</sup>Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger. <sup>18</sup>Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot. <sup>19</sup>Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil — this is the gift of God. <sup>20</sup>For he will not much remember the days of his life because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 opens in the sanctuary and closes in the field — from the fear of God to the gift of honest work. The Preacher is not changing the subject; he is showing us the spine of a life well-lived. The fear of God and the enjoyment of God’s gifts are not competing postures but complementary ones: reverence before God produces gratitude for his gifts; gratitude for his gifts deepens reverence before him.

The warning about worship (vv. 1–7) is startling in its directness. Religion is one of the places hebel hides most effectively. Words multiply, vows are made and broken, prayers are offered for show rather than from the heart, and the whole performance can feel like genuine worship while being, in God’s sight, the “sacrifice of fools.” The Preacher calls us to the radical simplicity of genuine encounter: draw near to listen, let your words be few, keep what you promise. God is in heaven; you are on earth. The difference matters.

Then comes the most pastoral observation in the chapter: the labourer sleeps sweetly (v. 12). Not the wealthy man, whose full stomach keeps him awake with anxiety. Wealth managed without God is not comfort but burden. But wealth received as gift from God, held loosely, enjoyed gratefully — this is the gift that makes sleep possible. Joy in the heart, given by God himself (v. 20), is the crown of a life oriented toward the One who gives it.

verseByVerse.quote: “To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher has visited the temple and seen what goes on there: hurried sacrifices offered without attention, prayers shaped more by performance than sincerity, the whole apparatus of religion deployed as a transaction rather than a meeting. He calls it the sacrifice of fools — not because sacrifice is foolish but because sacrifice without listening ear is worse than nothing. It is the audacity of approaching the King of the universe while barely noticing you are in his presence.

Jesus said almost the same thing in the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:9–14). The Pharisee’s words were many and impressive; the tax collector’s were few and honest. One went home justified; the other did not. The fear of God that produces few, careful words is not weakness but wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: “Pay what you vow.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vow-breaking was not a minor matter in the ancient world; it was a form of lying to God’s face. The Preacher’s advice is stark: better not to vow than to vow and not pay. The mouth that cannot keep its word before God is the mouth that has not truly grasped who God is. And God, the Preacher warns, will be angry at the voice that treats its commitments to him as negotiable.

This is not a counsel against commitment; it is a counsel toward seriousness of heart. Jesus said, “Let what you say be simply Yes or No” (Matt. 5:37). The life that fears God is the life that means what it says, especially before God. The one who kept every vow perfectly was Jesus himself, who said “not my will but yours be done” in Gethsemane and followed it to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: “Sweet is the sleep of a laborer.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the Preacher’s most charming observations. The wealthy man with the full stomach cannot sleep — he lies awake calculating, worrying, protecting. The labourer who ate little sleeps soundly. It is a small but luminous portrait of the difference between wealth held as master and wealth received as gift. The labourer trusts tomorrow to the same God who provided today. The wealthy man trusts tomorrow to his own management, and management never sleeps.

Jesus addressed this directly: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. 6:34). “Consider the lilies.” The peace that passes understanding (Phil. 4:7) is not the peace of having enough — it is the peace of knowing the God who gives enough. That peace makes sleep possible at any income level.

verseByVerse.quote: “Naked as he came, so shall he go.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher returns to the nakedness of death. You brought nothing into this world and you will take nothing out (cf. Job 1:21; 1 Tim. 6:7). The rich man who hoards for himself, loses it in a bad venture, and leaves his son with empty hands — this is not bad luck; it is the shape of life under the sun. Nothing accumulates past the grave.

This is not a text about the injustice of wealth but about the insufficiency of it as a foundation. Paul, who had learned contentment in plenty and in need (Phil. 4:11–12), understood what Qohelet is pointing toward: the life that is not built on perishable wealth but on imperishable grace is the life that faces death without being stripped. In Christ, you carry into eternity what no one can take away: the inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading (1 Pet. 1:4).

verseByVerse.quote: “God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes in sunlight. The gift of God is not escape from toil but joy in it — the ability to eat and drink and find genuine enjoyment in honest work, received as lot from God’s hand. And the final line is extraordinary: the person to whom God gives this joy does not spend much time calculating the days of their life, because God himself keeps them occupied with joy in their heart.

This is the New Testament doctrine of the fullness of the Spirit in embryo. The Spirit-filled life is not a life that has solved all its problems but a life so filled with the joy of God’s presence that anxiety cannot get a foothold. “You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Ps. 16:11). Qohelet glimpsed it; Pentecost made it available to all.

5.theology:
The Fear of the Lord as the Foundation of Wisdom. Proverbs declares that “the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 9:10), and Ecclesiastes ends with the same verdict (12:13). But chapter 5 shows us what the fear of the Lord looks like in practice: it is the posture that produces few words before God, kept vows, and gratitude for ordinary gifts. The fear of the Lord is not terror but awe — the recognition of the infinite distance between creature and Creator that, paradoxically, makes genuine intimacy possible.

Reformed theology has insisted that the fear of the Lord is not opposed to love for the Lord but is its necessary companion. John Calvin wrote that true piety “consists in a sincere feeling which loves God as Father as much as it fears and reverences him as Lord.” The Preacher’s counsel — let your words be few, keep your vows, receive joy as gift — is practical piety rooted in this double movement: reverence and love, awe and gratitude, fear and joy.
5.examples:
Then: Isaiah 1 is the prophetic version of Ecclesiastes 5:1: God tells his people that their sacrifices are an abomination because their hands are full of blood and their hearts are far from him. The ritual is present; the fear is absent. The temple has become a performance space rather than a meeting place. It is the sacrifice of fools on a national scale, and God will not receive it. The Preacher and the prophets are agreed: God prefers silence and sincerity to noise and show.

Now: Contemporary Christianity has its own versions of the sacrifice of fools: the eloquent prayer offered for the congregation’s applause, the worship song sung with perfect pitch and absent heart, the Christian social media post calibrated for likes rather than truth. The Preacher is not against beautiful worship — he is against worship that has forgotten who it is worshipping. Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. Slow down. Listen before you speak. Let your words be few and your heart be full. That is where you will find him.

6.title: The Appetite That Cannot Be Filled
6.text: <sup>1</sup>There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind: <sup>2</sup>a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil. <sup>3</sup>If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he. <sup>4</sup>For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered. <sup>5</sup>Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he. <sup>6</sup>Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good — do not all go to the one place? <sup>7</sup>All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied. <sup>8</sup>For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living? <sup>9</sup>Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind. <sup>10</sup>Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he. <sup>11</sup>The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage for man? <sup>12</sup>For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is the darkest passage in Ecclesiastes. The Preacher describes what he calls a “grievous evil”: a man who has everything — wealth, honour, a hundred children, two thousand years of life — and yet cannot enjoy any of it. The capacity for enjoyment has been withheld. He concludes, with shattering honesty, that such a man would be better off never having been born than a stillborn child finds rest.

This is not hyperbole. The Preacher is making a precise theological point: wealth without the God-given capacity to enjoy it is worthless. And the capacity for enjoyment — which he has already established is “from the hand of God” (2:24–25) — cannot be manufactured, purchased, or deserved. It is a gift. Which means the man who has everything but cannot enjoy it has missed the one thing that makes everything good: the God who gives and the posture of gratitude toward him.

The chapter ends with humanity’s epistemic limits laid bare: who knows what is good for man? Who can see beyond the shadow of this life? The Preacher cannot. And this honest unknowing points forward to the one who can — the one who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life (John 14:6), who came not only to give life but to give it abundantly (John 10:10). The appetite that no created thing can fill finds its satisfaction only in the one who is the Bread of Life.

verseByVerse.quote: “God does not give him power to enjoy them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scenario is deliberately extreme: maximum external blessing, zero internal enjoyment. A hundred children is the ancient world’s image of maximum prosperity (Job had ten; Solomon had seven hundred wives). Two thousand years of life surpasses every patriarch. And yet — the soul is not satisfied. The Preacher’s point is that God’s gifts are not self-contained; they are transparent to the Giver. Received from his hand with gratitude, they nourish. Accumulated and clutched, divorced from the relationship that makes them meaningful, they are inert.

Calvin wrote that created things are “the sparks of his glory.” The error is not in enjoying the sparks; it is in trying to warm yourself by a spark when the fire is available. The man with everything who cannot enjoy it has somehow acquired the sparks and lost sight of the fire.

verseByVerse.quote: “All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The image is visceral and true: all of human industry, from the first ploughed field to the latest quarterly earnings report, is ultimately aimed at feeding the mouth. And yet the appetite is never satisfied. Not because the food is bad — but because the mouth is not the deepest hunger. Beneath the physical appetite is a spiritual one that food cannot reach.

Jesus knew this when he quoted Deuteronomy to the tempter: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4). The deepest hunger is for the Word of God — for God himself. And Jesus, who declared himself the Bread of Life, promises that whoever comes to him will never hunger and whoever believes in him will never thirst (John 6:35). The appetite of chapter 6 finds its answer in John 6.

verseByVerse.quote: “Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
A deceptively simple proverb: what you can actually see and touch and enjoy in the present is better than the endlessly wandering appetite that is never satisfied by anything it achieves. This is not a counsel of lowered ambition but of present gratitude. The bird in hand is worth more than the fantasised flock on the horizon. Or in more theological terms: the present grace is better than the imagined future acquisition.

This is the practical wisdom of contentment that Paul describes in Philippians 4:11: “I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content.” Contentment is not passivity; it is the active reception of present grace as sufficient. The wandering appetite is the enemy of contentment — always pushing the satisfaction point one achievement further away.

verseByVerse.quote: “He is not able to dispute with one stronger than he.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever exists has already been named and defined by the Creator. Man did not name himself; he was named. Man did not define the terms of existence; they were defined. And the creature cannot take the Creator to court — cannot dispute the terms of his own existence with the One who brought him into being. The Preacher is making the same point God makes to Job from the whirlwind: “Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?” (Job 38:4).

This is humbling, but it is also liberating. If man cannot set the terms of his own existence, then man does not bear the burden of justifying his existence. That burden belongs to the one who named and created him. And the God who named us has also — in Christ — given us a new name, written in the Lamb’s book of life (Rev. 2:17). The strongest one does not oppress but redeems.

verseByVerse.quote: “For who knows what is good for man?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with the most searching question the Preacher has asked: who knows what is truly good for man during his brief, shadow-like life? And who can see what comes after? From under the sun, the answer is: no one. This is not nihilism — it is the proper limit of human knowledge, honestly stated.

But we read this as Christians. The one who knows what is good for man is the one who made him. And God, who “so loved the world that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16), has told us what is good through his Word, his Spirit, and supremely through the life of his Son. Jesus is the full revelation of what human life was made to be. Ecclesiastes 6:12 is the question; Matthew through John is the answer. The shadow-life finds its substance in him who is the Light of the world.

6.theology:
Common Grace and Saving Grace. Ecclesiastes 6 raises one of Reformed theology’s most important distinctions. God gives common grace to all — sun, rain, food, beauty, the capacity for reason and culture — to the righteous and unrighteous alike (Matt. 5:45). But the ability to enjoy these gifts as gifts, to receive them with gratitude as expressions of God’s fatherly love, is the fruit of saving grace and the regenerating work of the Holy Spirit.

The man in Ecclesiastes 6 who cannot enjoy his gifts is not receiving more judgment than another — he is simply revealing what life looks like when common grace is not received in the light of saving grace. The gifts are real; the capacity to enjoy them as gifts requires the relationship. This is why evangelism is not a subtraction from the enjoyment of life but its prerequisite. Knowing the Giver does not diminish the gifts; it transfigures them. Every meal eaten in fellowship with God is a eucharist. Every gift received with thanksgiving becomes an act of worship. Saving grace does not destroy common grace; it glorifies it.
6.examples:
Then: The book of Ecclesiastes itself is the literary evidence for chapter 6’s diagnosis. The Preacher has every gift available to ancient wisdom and power, and his great achievement is to observe their insufficiency with perfect lucidity. But the most striking Old Testament exemplar is Haman in the book of Esther: he has wealth, royal favour, a large family, the ear of the king — and one uncooperative Jew at the gate robs him of all enjoyment (Esther 5:13). “Yet all this is worth nothing to me.” The appetite was eating him alive.

Now: The modern version is the billionaire who has optimised every variable of life — nutrition, sleep, productivity, relationships — and still reports feeling empty. Or the person who achieves every goal on their ten-year plan and feels nothing when they arrive. Ecclesiastes 6 is not surprised. The diagnosis is precise: the capacity for enjoyment is not a function of external circumstances but of relationship with the God who gives. You cannot optimise your way to the joy only God can give. You can only receive it — with open, grateful, humble hands, from the one who holds all good things.

7.title: Wisdom's Bitter Beauty
7.text: <sup>1</sup>A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth. <sup>2</sup>It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart. <sup>3</sup>Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad. <sup>4</sup>The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. <sup>5</sup>It is better for a man to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools. <sup>6</sup>For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fools; this also is vanity. <sup>7</sup>Surely oppression drives the wise into madness, and a bribe corrupts the heart. <sup>8</sup>Better is the end of a thing than its beginning, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. <sup>9</sup>Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools. <sup>10</sup>Say not, “Why were the former days better than these?” for it is not from wisdom that you ask this. <sup>11</sup>Wisdom is good with an inheritance, an advantage to those who see the sun. <sup>12</sup>For the protection of wisdom is like the protection of money, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of him who has it. <sup>13</sup>Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked? <sup>14</sup>In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that man may not find out anything that will be after him. <sup>15</sup>In my vain life I have seen everything. There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evildoing. <sup>16</sup>Be not overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself? <sup>17</sup>Be not overly wicked, neither be a fool. Why should you die before your time? <sup>18</sup>It is good that you should take hold of this, and from that withhold not your hand, for the one who fears God shall come out from both of them. <sup>19</sup>Wisdom gives strength to the wise man more than ten rulers who are in a city. <sup>20</sup>Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins. <sup>21</sup>Do not take to heart all the things that people say, lest you hear your servant cursing you. <sup>22</sup>Your heart knows that many times you yourself have cursed others. <sup>23</sup>All this I have tested by wisdom. I said, “I will be wise,” but it was far from me. <sup>24</sup>That which is, is far off, and deep, very deep; who can find it out? <sup>25</sup>I turned my heart to know and to search out and to seek wisdom and the sum of things, and to know the wicked folly of foolishness and the foolishness that is madness. <sup>26</sup>And I find something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her. <sup>27</sup>“Behold, this is what I found,” says the Preacher, “adding one thing to one another to find the scheme of things — <sup>28</sup>which my soul has sought repeatedly, but I have not found. One man among a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I have not found. <sup>29</sup>See, this alone I found, that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes.”
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is a collection of proverbs strung together by the thread of wisdom’s counterintuitive nature. Again and again, the Preacher commends what the world avoids: the house of mourning over the house of feasting, the rebuke of the wise over the song of fools, the end of a thing over its beginning. Wisdom, he discovers, has a bitter edge — it requires going where the comfortable self resists going, and seeing what the satisfied eye refuses to see.

The great pivot of the chapter comes in verse 13: Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked? This is not resignation but theology. The crooked places in life — suffering, injustice, unanswered prayer, the righteous man perishing and the wicked man prospering — are not malfunctions in a broken machine. They are the work of a God who is doing something too large for us to see from inside the picture. Wisdom’s task is not to straighten what God has made crooked but to trust the Straightener.

The chapter ends with the Preacher’s most theologically concentrated verse: God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes (v. 29). This is the doctrine of original righteousness and the fall compressed into a single sentence. The crooked world of Ecclesiastes is not God’s original design; it is humanity’s departure from it. And the only one who has ever been found fully upright — without scheme, without deviation, without the bent of sin — is Jesus Christ, who is the righteousness of God incarnate (1 Cor. 1:30). In him, what was made crooked begins to be made straight again.

verseByVerse.quote: “It is better to go to the house of mourning.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the most uncomfortable pieces of wisdom in the Old Testament. The house of feasting is warm, well-lit, and full of laughter; the house of mourning is cold, dim, and full of weeping. And yet the Preacher says the mourning house is better — because it tells the truth. Death is the end of all mankind, and the person who has sat with it lays it to heart. The person who has never sat with it lives in a comfortable fiction.

Jesus said, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:4). He did not say blessed are those who laugh, though laughter is also a gift. He singled out mourners because mourning is the posture that makes comfort possible. You cannot be filled if you insist you are not empty. The house of mourning empties you; the gospel fills you. Sorrow is the preparation for joy, not its opposite.

verseByVerse.quote: “The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crackling of thorns under a pot is a vivid image: loud, bright, and gone in a moment, leaving nothing but ash. That is the laughter of fools — impressive noise with no lasting warmth. The Preacher sets against it the rebuke of the wise: uncomfortable, perhaps painful, but nourishing in ways that songs cannot be. Wisdom can receive correction; foolishness can only applaud itself.

Verse 10 is a pastoral treasure: “Do not ask, ‘Why were the former days better?’” Nostalgia is not wisdom; it is grief dressed up as discernment. The golden age was not as golden as memory insists, and more importantly, God’s best work is not necessarily behind you. The God who was faithful in the past is the God who is faithful now and will be faithful ahead. Patience faces forward; pride (and nostalgia) faces backward.

verseByVerse.quote: “God has made the one as well as the other.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher reaches one of his most important theological conclusions: both prosperity and adversity come from the hand of God, and they come together precisely so that man cannot predict or control his own future. This is not divine capriciousness; it is divine sovereignty wielded in love to keep his people dependent and humble. A God who only sent prosperity would produce a people who trusted their prosperity. The God who sends both keeps his people trusting him.

Verse 13 — who can make straight what he has made crooked? — is not a counsel of fatalism. It is a counsel of surrender to a wisdom larger than ours. The crooked thing in your life that you cannot straighten may be the very thing God is using to straighten you. Spurgeon wrote: “God is too good to be unkind and too wise to be mistaken.” The Preacher reaches the same conclusion from the other direction: stop trying to overrule God’s curriculum.

verseByVerse.quote: “There is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 20 is one of the most important statements in Ecclesiastes and one of the clearest anticipations of Romans 3:23: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” The Preacher has looked at the full range of human moral life and reached this verdict: no one is consistently righteous. Not the pious man, not the wise man, not the king. The righteous sometimes perish and the wicked sometimes prosper (v. 15) — and beneath both is the same root: every man and woman is a sinner.

The warning against “excessive righteousness” (v. 16) is not a counsel of moral mediocrity but a warning against self-righteous performance — the kind that destroys the person who practises it and repels everyone who observes it. The only righteousness that does not destroy is the righteousness received as gift — the righteousness of Christ credited to those who trust in him (2 Cor. 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: “God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher’s final verdict on his wisdom search is honest defeat: wisdom is “far from me” (v. 23). The sum of things is deep, very deep. No amount of searching from under the sun can reach the foundation. And then, in verse 29, a flash of theological brilliance: God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes. In one sentence, this is the doctrine of the fall. The problem is not God’s design — it was good, upright, beautiful. The problem is human scheming, the turning inward and downward that Genesis 3 describes.

This verse makes the gospel necessary and glorious. If man has bent himself through his own schemes, he cannot unbend himself through better schemes. He needs a Redeemer from outside the system — one who was himself upright without scheme or deviation, who took the full weight of human crookedness onto himself at the cross, and who is making all things new. Christ is the second Adam who reverses the schemes of the first.

7.theology:
Original Righteousness, the Fall, and the Doctrine of Sin. Ecclesiastes 7:29 is the clearest statement of original righteousness in the wisdom literature: God made humanity upright. Reformed theology has always insisted that the fall was a fall from something real and good — not from a neutral starting point but from genuine uprightness. Adam and Eve were not created morally neutral; they were created in the image of a holy God, with minds that knew him and wills that were bent toward him.

The “many schemes” humanity has sought since the fall are the alternative architectures of meaning and righteousness that every culture and every individual erects in God’s place. Ecclesiastes catalogues them: pleasure, achievement, wisdom, wealth, companionship. All good things. All insufficient replacements for God. The gospel does not merely forgive the schemes; it restores the uprightness — not through moral effort but through union with Christ, who is himself the upright Man, and through the renewing work of the Spirit who is making us into his image (2 Cor. 3:18).
7.examples:
Then: The hall of fame of Israel’s history is lined with people who learned wisdom’s bitter lessons through the house of mourning. Joseph’s suffering in the pit and the prison was the school that produced the wisdom to govern Egypt. David’s years as a fugitive in the wilderness produced the Psalms that have consoled the church for three millennia. The prophet Jeremiah, who wept more than anyone in the Old Testament, understood God’s heart for the nations more deeply than any other. The house of mourning is not a detour from wisdom; it is the curriculum.

Now: Our culture’s greatest fear is discomfort, and its highest value is positive feeling. We skip the house of mourning as fast as we can and fill the gap with entertainment, productivity, or therapy that promises to move us quickly back to functioning. The Preacher says: slow down. Sit with the sorrow. Let it do its work. The sadness of face that makes the heart glad (v. 3) is not depression — it is the honest confrontation with reality that creates space for genuine joy. You cannot receive resurrection comfort if you have not felt Good Friday grief.

8.title: In the Hand of God
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Who is like the wise? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed. <sup>2</sup>I say: Keep the king's command, because of God's oath to him. <sup>3</sup>Be not hasty to go from his presence. Do not take your stand in an evil cause, for he does whatever he pleases. <sup>4</sup>For the word of the king is supreme, and who may say to him, “What are you doing?” <sup>5</sup>Whoever keeps a command will know no evil thing, and the wise heart will know the proper time and the just way. <sup>6</sup>For there is a time and a way for everything, even though man's trouble lies heavy on him. <sup>7</sup>For he does not know what is to be, for who can tell him how it will be? <sup>8</sup>No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death.
